citations.review_text: Abysmal first impression. I've seen this game get glazed online, but when trying to launch the thing, I'm greeted my a settings menu that doesn't work and a cinematic with no audio.

A terrible PC port that forces you to fix the game before you can even play it

The game launches in windowed mode, and the problems only get worse from there.

It comes with several ridiculous issues by default. Cutscenes play without voices, and mouse sensitivity is initially set to zero, meaning the camera simply does not move until you identify the problem and manually fix it.

The settings menu does not work properly either. I can highlight certain options, but whenever I press Enter to change them, the game switches back to windowed mode. It makes adjusting the settings almost impossible and, to make matters worse, it changes my graphics settings and sets everything to the lowest possible quality.

I started a new game hoping I could fix these problems through the in-game options. Instead, the opening cutscene played without voices and suffered from major graphical glitches: the vehicles were transparent, allowing me to see the characters inside them. I eventually skipped the cutscene because watching it in that state was pointless.

The PC controls are also awful. It is painfully obvious that the game was designed to be played with a controller, yet it does not even allow you to remap the controls. You are forced to use an outdated, unintuitive button layout that makes the entire game feel mechanically clumsy and unresponsive.

Aesthetically, this game has everything it needs to be something I could enjoy. Unfortunately, between the awkward controls and all the time I have already wasted identifying and fixing problems that exist by default, I am now getting dangerously close to the refund time limit.

I would rather get my money back than keep giving it more chances. If the beginning of the game is this poorly handled, I have no reason to trust that I will not encounter another bug halfway through the campaign that ruins the experience completely.

Refund requested.

basic menus are broken, like the settings menu. started a new game to see if the in game menu was different. there was no audio with the opening cutscene and the menus were still broken. sucks, this looked fun.

This game instantly shows that it's little more than a glorified walking loot grinding simulator. It's the driving equivalent of a walking simulator at least. We're instantly assaulted with the idea that we need to scavenge for water, fuel and parts along with other stuff like ammo and that we need to drive around raiding camps to get more resources.

This kind of game rubs me the wrong way after being exposed to its ilk far too many times. It feels unimaginative, a way to stretch what should've been a 10 hour game tops into 50+ hours of useless "side questing". The game is essentially just collecting crap, beating crazy sand pygmies into submission, or rather the next life, unlocking upgrades and upgrading our car to compensate for the protagonist's tiny gonads with wheels of death.

I would've given it more of a chance if the it was less grindy and more story.

The story seems to be pretty fun but I'm not about to sit through all that grinding and useless driving for so little reward only to upgrade a vehicle and progress through an edgy story.

Also, it leaves a bitter taste when the first thing you're met with are several bugs. The main menu settings doesn't work and if you use it, it goes blank afterwards. Entering the game makes these settings available though, but if you ever click the main menu settings instead of doing it from the game, it will reset all settings to default. Then there was no sound as for some reason the cinematic sound was set to 0, almost dropped it right there.

We're then quickly shoved into a game where the protagonist somehow befriends an overly intelligent rabid dog and then you meet some kind of gollum wannabe religious fanatic mechanic that believes the protagonist is a saint.

It's so over the top I'm not sure what to say. I'd be lying if I said it wasn't interesting, but once again, I'm not about to spend 30-60 hours wasting my time driving around collecting scrap to upgrade my wiener while pretending to be badass only for some s…

claims.claim: Reviewers report that the hand-to-hand combat system resembles the style used in the Batman Arkham games, featuring counters, heavy punches, and brutal executions.

citations.review_text:
Mad Max is one of those post apocalyptic open world games that is very easy to overlook.

The gameplay is surprisingly addictive. Most of the activities revolve around the Magnum Opus and your car in general. You snipe enemies from a distance, destroy towers, clear minefields, upgrade the car, fight convoys, race across the wasteland, and improve Max himself.

For me, the vehicle gameplay is the real heart of Mad Max. The convoy battles are easily the best part of the game. Chasing a convoy through the desert while smashing enemy cars, using the harpoon, firing the shotgun, and trying to destroy the lead vehicle feels great. It is also something I do not see often in other open world games. As someone who loves Mad Max: Fury Road, these sequences capture that same feeling of chaos on the road better than I expected.

Hand to hand combat is also very satisfying. Every punch feels heavy and brutal. The basic system reminds me of the Batman Arkham games, but it is simpler, rougher, and much more violent. Max does not fight like a superhero. He fights like someone trying to survive.

The story is probably the weakest part of the game. There simply is not that much going on for most of the campaign. The main missions often feel more like another reason to travel somewhere, fight some enemies, and keep moving.

It is only around the last quarter of the game that the story starts to dig deeper into Max as a character and delivers some genuinely strong emotional moments. Before that, Max mostly feels like a strange driver wandering through the wasteland, helping people when it benefits him and then moving on.

Mad Max is not a game I would recommend for its story. I would recommend it for the wasteland, the cars, the brutal combat, and especially the convoy battles.

If you enjoyed Fury Road and want an open world game built around surviving and driving through that kind of wasteland, this is still worth playing.

Its a Warner Bro's game, so the fighting  style is similar to Batman Arkham games and Shadow of War, easy to adapt. It also reminds me a little of Twisted Metal when colliding with other vehicles, there are different ways to upgrade your vehicle and attack. Graphics hold out good for a game from 2015.

Mad Max (2015) in 2026, and I can honestly say it's still an old but gold game.

The graphics, action, and gameplay are amazing, especially considering its age. Some of the cutscenes don't feel as smooth by today's standards, but that's completely understandable for a game released in 2015.

The game is a bit grindy, and it might feel repetitive at the beginning. However, if you stick with it and keep progressing, the overall experience becomes much more enjoyable and rewarding.

The storyline feels like watching an action movie, which kept me engaged from start to finish. Even in 2026, I think Mad Max is a great choice if you're looking for a fun single-player game to pass the time.

⭐ Rating: 9.5/10

citations.review_text:
Mad Max is one of those post apocalyptic open world games that is very easy to overlook.

The gameplay is surprisingly addictive. Most of the activities revolve around the Magnum Opus and your car in general. You snipe enemies from a distance, destroy towers, clear minefields, upgrade the car, fight convoys, race across the wasteland, and improve Max himself.

For me, the vehicle gameplay is the real heart of Mad Max. The convoy battles are easily the best part of the game. Chasing a convoy through the desert while smashing enemy cars, using the harpoon, firing the shotgun, and trying to destroy the lead vehicle feels great. It is also something I do not see often in other open world games. As someone who loves Mad Max: Fury Road, these sequences capture that same feeling of chaos on the road better than I expected.

Hand to hand combat is also very satisfying. Every punch feels heavy and brutal. The basic system reminds me of the Batman Arkham games, but it is simpler, rougher, and much more violent. Max does not fight like a superhero. He fights like someone trying to survive.

The story is probably the weakest part of the game. There simply is not that much going on for most of the campaign. The main missions often feel more like another reason to travel somewhere, fight some enemies, and keep moving.

It is only around the last quarter of the game that the story starts to dig deeper into Max as a character and delivers some genuinely strong emotional moments. Before that, Max mostly feels like a strange driver wandering through the wasteland, helping people when it benefits him and then moving on.

Mad Max is not a game I would recommend for its story. I would recommend it for the wasteland, the cars, the brutal combat, and especially the convoy battles.

If you enjoyed Fury Road and want an open world game built around surviving and driving through that kind of wasteland, this is still worth playing.

**The joke:**
I started Mad Max thinking, “I’m going to become the king of the wasteland.”
Five minutes later, I was driving around collecting scrap like a post-apocalyptic garbage man. 😂🔥

**The facts:**
Mad Max is seriously underrated. The game delivers exactly what you'd want from a Mad Max experience: brutal vehicle combat, satisfying hand-to-hand fights, massive explosions, and a huge wasteland that is just begging to be explored.

The driving and car customization are easily some of the best parts. Upgrading the Magnum Opus actually feels meaningful, and turning your battered car into an absolute monster is incredibly satisfying.

The melee combat is also surprisingly fun, with heavy punches, counters, executions, and that satisfying feeling of beating the living daylights out of anyone who gets too close.

The atmosphere is fantastic, the wasteland looks incredible, and the overall gameplay loop of exploring, fighting, upgrading, and causing maximum chaos is ridiculously addictive.

Is it perfect? No. But is it **way more fun than it gets credit for? Absolutely.**

9/10.

[h1]It’s Mad Max - Now with 1000% More Grind![/h1]

Launched on the exact same day as [i]Metal Gear Solid V[/i] back in 2015, [i]Mad Max[/i] was largely overlooked at release and written off by critics as just a “generic open-world collectathon”… which it is! But over the last decade, it has built a strong cult following as one of the ultimate "comfort games" of the 2010s.

[h1]The Wasteland & Atmosphere[/h1]
The graphics hold up remarkably well for a 2015 game, especially when dynamic sandstorms sweep across the map to wreak absolute havoc. The atmosphere is further enhanced by a day/night cycle that actively shifts the danger: standard Roadkill and Scrotus' War Boys roam the roads by day, while the far more terrifying Buzzards take over at sunset.

[h1]The Magnum Opus & Car Combat[/h1]
Vehicular gameplay is where this game truly shines. Transforming the ‘Magnum Opus’ from a stripped-down chassis into an all-out war machine is deeply satisfying. Whether you’re harpooning tires, blowing up fuel tanks, or hunting down convoys, having your hunchbacked mechanic Chumbucket blast rockets at "infidels" (in Chum’s words) while screeching holy praise to the “combustion engine gods” is easily a highlight of the game.

[h1]On-Foot Combat & Brawling[/h1]
When you step out of the car, [i]Mad Max[/i] "borrows" the free-flowing combat system straight from the [i]Batman: Arkham[/i] series. However, it swaps out Batman's smooth martial arts precision for raw, brutal, back-alley street-fight violence. The brawling really packs a punch, featuring everything from arm bars to suplexes while also featuring shiv takedowns and of course point-blank shotgun blasts.

[h1]The Bad: The Grind & Map Bloat[/h1]
Where the game stumbles most is its pacing. Like most open-world games from that era, by the 15-hour mark the loop of destroying scarecrows, clearing sniper towers, and sniffing out landmines gets painfully repetitive. The story itself is paper-thin, and the campaign routinely halts your …

One of the most underrated games I've ever played. I went into Mad Max expecting a decent licensed game. Instead, I ended up spending way too many hours driving around the wasteland, beating raiders to death, and turning my car into a rolling war crime. The combat is basically Batman: Arkham if Batman traded his cape and gadgets for a shotgun, a leather jacket, and decades of unresolved trauma. The free-flow combat feels fantastic, the counters are satisfying, and every finishing move looks like it was approved by an orthopedic surgeon who wanted more business. Every fight ends with someone questioning whether bones were ever meant to bend that way. The vehicle combat is just as addictive. I kept telling myself, "Just one more convoy," and suddenly it was 2 a.m. and I was ramming dipsh*ts off cliffs with a supercharged death machine that Chumbucket somehow says "still needs a few upgrades." The world absolutely nails the Mad Max atmosphere. It's somehow beautiful and completely miserable at the same time. Every abandoned highway, rusted shipwreck, and dust storm makes you feel like civilization didn't just collapse, it exploded and took the instruction manual with it. Is it repetitive? Sure. So is going to work everyday without eating the barrel of a 12-guage , and somehow I still keep doing that too. If you've ever wanted to feel like Batman after a really, really bad day, while driving the angriest car ever built, this game is for you. Criminally underrated, ridiculously fun, and easily one of my favorite open-world games.

Try to go up a hillside and your car struggles to move five inches, while fishtailing randomly with every bump.

HAND-TO-HAND COMBAT: The combat sequences play much like Batman Arkham games or Spider-Man games: Punch, block, dodge. You need to block at the right time and dodge at the right time. You can pick up melee weapons, which break after a few swings but do more damage. After landing several blows, Max enters Fury mode, in which his swings become wilder, inflict more damage, and have new animations. Learn skills to instantly dispatch enemies, or stab them with knives. Until... you start realizing that their block controls just randomly fail; you can press the Block button and still get punched, because it just ignores the input. (The game tells you that you can't block while in the middle of a Heavy attack, but it also just fails to block at random even when you aren't doing anything else.) You can use your shotgun in an emergency to kill an enemy instantly... until you can't; some enemies just don't take any damage from the shotgun. The combat should be fun but instead it's frustrating.

I keep coming back to this game in my head. Was it a perfect game? No, it has some pretty significant limitations; it very much suffers from the 'Ubisoft Syndrome'. Towers to climb, fun locked behind progression, and exploration turned into a neccesary chore rather than offered as a reward for the curious. And yet, there's something about it that has stuck with me for years.

It's been out long enough now that I feel like reviewing the gameplay is moot, it has really good car combat, it's story is okay, it's characters are okay... But there is one element which is, in my opinion, simultaneuously the games greatest strength, and also it's Achile's Heel; the silence of the late game.

Breaking camps can be a challenge, destroying convoys is a huge amount of fun, pulling down sniper towers with the sniper still in them is incredibly satisfying... But once you've done that, they don't come back...

Once you're in the post ending game world, the wasteland is just... empty, a lot of the time. The Buzzards and the Roadkill don't provide the same challenge, and they tend to flee from late-game players, because they know they don't stand a chance... So a lot of my time in the late game is just... driving around, experiencing the emptiness...

Which is not a lot of fun, and makes some of the combat achievements basicly impossible to get without starting a new game, but there's also something disturbingly right about it. 

Max doesn't create, he destroys. Imortal Joe's faction is antithetical to what modern society says is 'right', so destroying them is justified. But by destroying them, we're not fixing the problem, merely setting the world state back to zero, and Max isn't going to stick around to see what the world he has shaped will turn into. 

So, an empty game-world is not very rewarding to the player, but then, what other ending could Mad Max have ever had?
